title: Despised and cleansed (section 16)
hook: if someone is scorned for keeping this teaching, past wrongs are wiped away

segments.voice: Yesterday: carrying the sutra. Those who copy, keep, recite and explain it carry awakening on their shoulders. Your line: on your shoulders. Did you pass one line along? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

The eye-roll lands before the sentence is even finished. Someone at the table mentions that they've started sitting quietly every morning, or reading an old sutra on the train, and a cousin snorts. Somebody else changes the subject. It's small. It stings anyway. Section sixteen of the Diamond Sutra looks straight at that sting. It doesn't promise that keeping this teaching will make you admired. It says the opposite might happen, and then it says something surprising about what the scorn does. Today: despised and cleansed.

First, the scorn. The Buddha tells Subhuti that a good man or a good woman might receive this sutra, keep it, read it, recite it, and be despised by others for it. The sutra doesn't pretend that won't happen. Second, the reason it gives. That person, the sutra says, carries wrongs from former lives, deeds heavy enough to lead to a painful rebirth. But because they are scorned in this life, those past wrongs are wiped away, and they will reach awakening. The scorn, in this picture, isn't a punishment piling on. It's an old debt being settled in a lighter coin. That's the sutra's way of reading karma: deeds ripen, and sometimes they ripen small. Third, the comparison. The Buddha remembers his own long past, before he met the earlier Buddha Dipankara. He says he served and honored a vast number of buddhas, and missed none of them. Even so, he says, the merit of all that service doesn't come close to the merit of someone in a later age who keeps and recites this sutra. Fourth, the limit. If he told the whole of that merit, the Buddha says, some who heard it would be bewildered and doubt it. So he stops. The meaning of this sutra is beyond thought, and so is its fruit. Notice what the section does not say. It doesn't say scorn is good, or that anyone should seek it out, or that people who mock are villains. It simply says that a slight, borne quietly by someone keeping the teaching, can do a kind of washing. That's a very different thing from shrugging off harm. A sideways look at the dinner table is one thing. Cruelty is another, and nothing here asks anyone to stay inside it.
screen: `DESPISED FOR KEEPING IT.` · `OLD WRONGS WIPED AWAY.` · `MORE THAN SERVING BUDDHAS.` · `BEYOND THOUGHT.` · then, large: `CLEANSED BY SCORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: bear one small scorn. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you keep that someone once made light of: a habit, a hope, a quiet practice, a faith, maybe this one. Let the remark come back in its own words, small and a little sharp. Then, instead of a comeback, let the out-breath be the whole reply. Hear it again; breathe out again. Each time, picture yourself carrying on with the thing you keep, unhurried, as if the remark had passed like weather. Keep it to small slights; if something real and painful comes up, set it aside and simply follow the breath. The bell holds the time.
Despised and cleansed. Section sixteen says that when someone keeping this sutra is scorned, past wrongs are wiped away. Today's word.
Your line: cleansed by scorn. Today, if a small slight comes your way, let it pass through without a comeback, and notice whether it weighs less by evening. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers sometimes read section 16 as a way to meet ridicule with patience: the slight is understood as old karma ripening lightly, borne without retaliation.

myth: section 16 says scorn is good and should be sought out
it never says to seek scorn; it says scorn borne while keeping the teaching wipes away past wrongs.
the Buddha says keeping this sutra outweighs his service to countless buddhas
the merit of his long service doesn't come close, he says.
the Buddha lays out the whole merit in detail
he stops, saying some would be bewildered; the meaning is beyond thought.

fork.setup: you're keeping the sutra, and someone scorns you for it. what does section 16 say the scorn does?
options: proves you're on the wrong path
wipes away wrongs from former lives
earns you the right to scorn back
fork.reveal: the sutra says past deeds that would have led to painful rebirth are wiped away, and that person will reach awakening.

original.note: Sanskrit: deed, action; section 16 reads scorn as past deeds ripening in a lighter form.

trapdoor: what you thought: being despised means you've failed.
what it means: the sutra says scorn borne while keeping the teaching wipes old wrongs away.
what a scholar hears: karma ripening small now instead of heavy later, set beside the merit of serving countless buddhas.

notes: Section 16 paraphrased, not quoted (Max Müller's wording unverified): check the scorn of those who keep the sutra, past deeds leading to painful rebirth wiped away, the Buddha's service to buddhas before Dipankara 'missing none', the comparison of merit, and the line that hearers would be bewildered.
The vast number of buddhas served is given in the sutra; it is left unstated here under the claims rule.
'An old debt settled in a lighter coin' and the closing distinction between a slight and cruelty are the writer's framing, added so the practice can't be read as endorsing abuse; confirm the tone.

Editor pass: the practice (recall a slight, find it in the jaw/chest) repeated day 1131's practice almost exactly; it now recalls being made light of for something one keeps and answers with the out-breath, with the guard against painful memories kept.
